learning.learning_goal: Understand perimeter as the total distance around a two-dimensional boundary, measured in linear units.
learning.big_idea: Perimeter measures a boundary path: trace every outside segment exactly once and total their lengths.
assumed_prior_knowledge: recognize the outside edge of a shape
novice_success_criteria: distinguish boundary distance from interior coverage
trace every outside segment exactly once
total side lengths and label the answer in linear units

screens.label: Lesson 009 · Prototype
screens.title: How far is it around the outside?
screens.body: Imagine walking along every outside edge and returning to where you started. Perimeter is the total distance of that complete trip.
screens.callout: No perimeter formula is assumed. We will build the measurement by tracing one full trip around.

screens.label: Misconception
screens.title: Fencing does not measure the space inside.
screens.prompt: A rectangular garden needs fencing along every outside edge. What must be measured?

choices.text: The flat ground covered inside the garden
The complete distance around the outside boundary
choices.feedback: Fencing follows the boundary, so every outside side length must be included exactly once.

choices.text: Only the longest side

hints: Imagine walking where the fence will go.
A complete trip must return to the starting point.

screens.label: Observe
screens.title: Trace one complete trip around the boundary.

visual.ariaLabel: A rectangle five units wide and three units high with its outside boundary emphasized
visual.caption: Start → 5 across → 3 down → 5 back → 3 up
visual.message: Every outside segment is counted once, and the path ends where it started.

screens.label: Discover
screens.title: Which total represents the full boundary?

visual.ariaLabel: A five-by-three rectangle with all four outside sides labeled
visual.message: Opposite sides have matching lengths: 5, 3, 5, and 3 units.

choices.text: 5 × 3 = 15 square units because multiplication measures the covered space inside
5 + 3 = 8 units

choices.feedback: A complete boundary includes both long sides and both short sides.

hints: List each side as you trace around once.
Do not stop after reaching only two sides.

screens.label: Language
screens.title: Name the boundary, unit, and measurement.

visual.ariaLabel: A rectangle four units wide and two units high with a highlighted boundary

screens.phraseMeaning: The total one-dimensional distance around a two-dimensional shape

definitions.meaning: the outside edge that separates a shape from the space around it
a unit such as a foot or meter that measures distance in one direction
the total length of one complete path around a shape

screens.guidance: Before calculating, ask: Am I measuring the inside coverage or tracing the outside boundary?

screens.label: Remember
screens.title: Start, trace once, return, total.
screens.hook: Perimeter = one complete trip around the outside.
screens.body: Rebuild the measurement from the boundary path instead of choosing a formula by keyword.
rebuildSteps: Choose a starting point on the outside edge.
Trace every outside segment exactly once.
Return to the starting point without skipping or repeating a side.
Add the segment lengths and label the answer in ordinary linear units.
screens.boundary: Adding twice the length and twice the width works for rectangles. Irregular shapes require tracing and totaling every outside segment that actually exists.

screens.label: Symbol
screens.title: Which statement explains a 6-by-2 rectangle?

visual.ariaLabel: A rectangle six units wide and two units high with all four boundary sides labeled
visual.message: The boundary contains sides of 6, 2, 6, and 2 units.

choices.text: 6 × 2 = 12 square units because multiplying the dimensions counts the entire covered region inside
6 + 2 + 6 + 2 = 16 units for the complete outside trace
choices.feedback: The sum follows one complete trip around the rectangle and uses linear units.

choices.text: 6 + 2 = 8 units because each dimension is counted once

hints: Write the side lengths in travel order.
A rectangle has two sides of each dimension.

screens.label: Reveal
screens.title: The formula is a compressed boundary trace.

visual.ariaLabel: A six-by-two rectangle showing a complete sixteen-unit boundary
visual.message: Two widths and two heights form the complete outside path.

screens.label: Guided practice
screens.title: Trace a boundary that is not a rectangle.
screens.prompt: The stepped shape has six outside segments. What is its perimeter?

visual.ariaLabel: A stepped shape with six boundary segments labeled 6, 2, 2, 2, 4, and 4 units
visual.message: Start at the dot and trace all six outside segments: 6, 2, 2, 2, 4, and 4 units.

choices.text: 16 units, because the inward step can be skipped
24 square units, because 6 × 4 measures the inside
20 units, because 6 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 4 + 4 traces the complete boundary
choices.feedback: The inward step is still part of the outside boundary, so all six segments total 20 units.

hints: Follow the blue line without jumping across the inward step.
List every segment in travel order before adding.

screens.label: Independent practice
screens.title: Reason without the model.
screens.prompt: A rectangular picture frame is 8 inches wide and 5 inches high. How much trim goes around it?

choices.text: 40 square inches, because 8 × 5 counts the rectangular picture surface inside the frame
26 inches, because 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 traces the frame
choices.feedback: Trim follows the outside boundary, so the total is 26 linear inches.

choices.text: 13 inches, because 8 + 5 uses the two given numbers

hints: The trim must reach all four sides.
A frame measures boundary distance, not interior coverage.

screens.label: Recall
screens.title: Reconstruct perimeter from its meaning.
screens.prompt: Why is perimeter reported in ordinary units rather than square units?

choices.text: Because it measures a one-dimensional distance along the boundary
choices.feedback: The path has length but does not cover a two-dimensional region.

choices.text: Because perimeter counts all the equal square units covering the inside region
Because ordinary units are used only for rectangles

hints: Think about what a measuring tape follows.
A boundary path extends along one direction at a time.

screens.label: Transfer
screens.title: Separate equal area from boundary distance.
screens.prompt: A 3-by-8 rectangle and a 4-by-6 rectangle each have area 24 square units. Which needs more edging?

choices.text: They need the same amount of edging because equal areas always create equal outside boundaries
The 3-by-8 rectangle: its perimeter is 22 units, compared with 20 units
choices.feedback: Equal coverage does not force equal boundary distance; the dimensions determine the trip around.

choices.text: The 4-by-6 rectangle because 4 is greater than 3

hints: Trace and total all four sides of each rectangle.

screens.label: Reflect
screens.title: Which explanation shows understanding?
screens.prompt: Choose the statement that explains perimeter.

choices.text: Perimeter counts equal squares covering the inside.
Perimeter is found by multiplying any two side lengths.
Perimeter totals one complete path around the outside boundary.

hints: Think about fencing, trim, or edging.
A complete path returns to its starting point.

screens.title: You separated boundary distance from coverage.
screens.body: You connected the outside path, side lengths, linear units, and the contrast between perimeter and area.
screens.nextRecommendation: Review area and perimeter together, then test the distinction in an unfamiliar setting.
